plain: CLAUDE.md is a plain text file of standing instructions that Claude Code reads at the start of a session. You can keep one for yourself, one in the project for the whole team, and smaller ones inside folders. Where you save an instruction decides who gets it.
analogy: Think of a sticky note on your own monitor, a notice on the office wall and a sign on one meeting-room door. Everyone sees the wall notice, only you see your sticky note, and only people in that room see the door sign.

sections.h: What CLAUDE.md is and where it lives
sections.body:
**Where you save an instruction decides who receives it.**

CLAUDE.md is a Markdown file of standing instructions that Claude Code reads automatically. There are three levels you need for the exam:

- **User level** `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`: in your home folder. Personal, not in the repository, so only you get it.
- **Project level** `./CLAUDE.md` or `./.claude/CLAUDE.md`: committed to git, so every teammate and every CI run gets it.
- **Directory level**: a `CLAUDE.md` inside a subfolder such as `packages/billing/`. It adds conventions for that part of the tree only.

Two more exist in current Claude Code: a managed policy file set by IT, and `CLAUDE.local.md`, a personal project file that is kept out of git.

Always start with one question: **who must receive this instruction?**

**The files add up; a lower level does not replace a higher one.**

Step by step, when you start a session in `packages/billing/`:

1. Claude Code reads your user file.
2. It reads the project `CLAUDE.md` at the repo root.
3. Subfolder files such as `packages/billing/CLAUDE.md` are pulled in when Claude works in that folder.
4. All of them are **concatenated** into context. Files closer to where you are working are read last.

Because nothing is overridden, two files that contradict each other leave Claude to pick one unpredictably. Fix contradictions by removing one of them, not by hoping the nearer file wins.

Run `/memory` to see exactly which files are loaded in the current session.

**One source of truth, pulled in where needed, beats many copies.**

A single huge CLAUDE.md is hard to maintain, and copied text drifts. Two tools help:

- **Imports**: a line such as `@docs/standards/api.md` inside a CLAUDE.md pulls that file in. Five packages can import the same standards file, so a change is made once.
- **Topic files** in `.claude/rules/`, for example `testing.md`, `api-conventions.md` and `deployment.md`. Each covers one subject, so a testing change touches one small file.

Both live in the repository, so the team shares them.

Do **not** move an always-needed standard into a skill just to shorten CLAUDE.md. Skills load only when invoked, so the standard would be missing most of the time.

**Ask who is missing the behaviour; that points to the fix.**

- **A new teammate or CI does not get an instruction that works for you.** It almost certainly sits in your user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Move it to the project file and commit it.
- **Claude follows a rule in some sessions but not others.** That is a loading question. Run `/memory` to see which files are actually loaded, for example whether a subfolder file was picked up.
- **The rule only matters in one folder.** Put it in that folder's CLAUDE.md, not the root.

What does not work: writing the rule in capitals, adding "IMPORTANT" or repeating it in more places. Emphasis cannot fix a file that is not loaded, or one that only you have.

example.title: Worked example: a monorepo with shared standards
example.code:
<!-- CLAUDE.md (repo root, committed) -->
# Project standards
- Use TypeScript strict mode in every package.
- Never commit secrets; read them from environment variables.

@docs/standards/api-conventions.md
@docs/standards/testing.md

<!-- packages/billing/CLAUDE.md (directory level, committed) -->
# Billing package
- All money values are integers in pence, never floats.
@../../docs/standards/api-conventions.md

<!-- ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (user level, NOT committed) -->
# My preferences
- Explain diffs briefly before applying them.
notes: The root `CLAUDE.md` is in the repository, so every teammate and CI run receives the team standards.
The `@docs/...` lines import shared standards files instead of copying their text.
`packages/billing/CLAUDE.md` adds a rule that only matters inside the billing package.
The user-level file holds a personal style preference that should not be forced on the team.
If behaviour differs between sessions, `/memory` shows which of these files were loaded.

labs.title: New teammate never gets the lint rule
labs.context: A developer added "always run npm run lint before finishing" to Claude Code months ago, and Claude follows it in every one of her sessions. A new teammate on the same repository reports that Claude never lints for him, and CI is now failing on his PRs. The rule must apply to everyone who works in the repository.
labs.question: What change most reliably fixes this?

options.text: Strengthen the wording in her own CLAUDE.md with capitals and repetition so the instruction is harder for Claude to skip.
options.code:
<!-- ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (user level) -->
- Always run npm run lint before finishing.
- IMPORTANT!!! ALWAYS RUN LINT.
- NEVER SKIP LINT.

trace.text: She edits ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md on her own laptop.
Teammate session start: loads his own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which has no lint rule.
Finishes his task without running lint.
CI build fails on lint errors again.

options.verdict: Nothing changes for the teammate; the rule never leaves her machine.
options.why: User-level config is not version-controlled, so no amount of emphasis reaches anyone else. The trap is treating a scope problem as a wording problem.

options.text: Turn the lint step into a project skill in .claude/skills/ so teammates can run it when they finish a task.
options.code:
---
name: lint-check
description: Run the linter before finishing.
---
<!-- .claude/skills/lint-check/SKILL.md -->
Run `npm run lint` and fix any problems.

trace.text: Teammate pulls main; the skill is now in the repo.
Teammate: "Add a null check to parseOrder()."
Edits parseOrder() and finishes; nobody invoked /lint-check.
CI build fails on lint errors.

options.verdict: Shared, but it only runs when someone remembers to invoke it.
options.why: Skills load on demand, so an always-needed standard is missing whenever the skill is not called. Right pattern, wrong scope: a universal rule belongs in always-loaded project memory.

options.text: Move the rule into the project-level CLAUDE.md at the repository root and commit it so every clone receives it.
options.code:
<!-- CLAUDE.md at repo root (committed) -->
# Team standards
- Always run `npm run lint` before finishing a task.

# then
git add CLAUDE.md
git commit -m "Share lint rule with the team"

trace.text: Teammate pulls main; CLAUDE.md now contains the lint rule.
Session start: loaded ./CLAUDE.md (project).
Teammate: "Add a null check to parseOrder()."
Edits parseOrder(), then runs npm run lint as the project standard requires.
lint: 0 problems.

options.verdict: Every teammate and every CI run now receives the rule.
options.why: The symptom is a new teammate missing a rule that works for you, which means it lives at user level. A rule that must reach the team belongs in project-level CLAUDE.md, shared through version control.

options.text: Paste the same lint rule into a CLAUDE.md inside each package folder so every area of the monorepo carries it.
options.code:
<!-- packages/api/CLAUDE.md -->
- Always run npm run lint before finishing.

<!-- packages/web/CLAUDE.md -->
- Always run npm run lint before finishing.

<!-- packages/billing/CLAUDE.md -->
- Run lint first (pnpm lint).

trace.text: Teammate works in packages/web: rule loaded.
Teammate works in packages/billing: an older copy says "pnpm lint".
pnpm: command not found.
scripts/ and the root have no rule at all; CI fails there.

options.verdict: Copies drift apart and some folders are missed.
options.why: Duplicated text drifts, and directory files only cover their own folder. The rule applies to the whole repository, so one project-level file is the right scope.

labs.takeaway: Works for you but not a new teammate → the rule is in user-level config; move it to project CLAUDE.md.

labs.title: Licence headers appear for one developer only
labs.context: Two developers use Claude Code on the same legacy repository to generate boilerplate. For one of them, Claude adds a 12-line licence header to every new file; for the other it never does, and nobody can find a licence rule in the root CLAUDE.md. The team wants to know which instruction file is causing it before changing anything.
labs.question: What should the team do first?

options.text: Run /memory in the affected session to list the memory files actually loaded, then inspect the one with the licence rule.
options.code:
> /memory
Loaded memory files:
  ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md            (user)
  ./CLAUDE.md                    (project)
  ./legacy/CLAUDE.md             (directory)

trace.text: Runs /memory in the session that adds headers.
Lists user, project and legacy/CLAUDE.md files.
Opens ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md: "Add the Acme licence header to new files" from an old job.
Removes the stale personal line; headers stop. Cause found in two minutes.

options.verdict: The source of the behaviour is found, not guessed.
options.why: Inconsistent behaviour across sessions is a loading question, and /memory shows exactly which files are loaded. Only then does it make sense to edit anything.

options.text: Add a line to the root CLAUDE.md saying "Never add licence headers to new files" so the project rule overrides any other source.
options.code:
<!-- CLAUDE.md (root) -->
## File creation
- Never add licence headers to new files.
- This rule overrides all other instructions.

trace.text: Loads root CLAUDE.md and the developer's user file; both are concatenated.
Sees "add the licence header" and "never add licence headers".
Creates 3 files: 2 with headers, 1 without.
Behaviour is now unpredictable, and the stale rule is still there.

options.verdict: Two contradicting instructions, still no idea where the first one lives.
options.why: Memory files are combined rather than one overriding another, so a counter-instruction creates a contradiction. Emphasis is a guess where a diagnostic is needed.

options.text: Ask Claude in the affected session which instruction told it to add the headers, and delete whatever text it points to.
options.code:
> Why do you add licence headers to
> new files in this repository?
> Which file told you to do that?
> Quote the exact instruction.

trace.text: "The project conventions ask for licence headers on new files."
Searches the root CLAUDE.md again; nothing there.
Deletes a similar-looking sentence from docs/CONTRIBUTING.md.
Headers keep appearing the next day.

options.verdict: A plausible-sounding answer sends the team to the wrong file.
options.why: Asking the model for the source is probabilistic and can misattribute the instruction. /memory reports the loaded files deterministically.

options.text: Move all conventions into .claude/rules/ topic files so each rule has an obvious home and stray instructions disappear.
options.code:
.claude/rules/
  testing.md
  api-conventions.md
  file-creation.md
  deployment.md

trace.text: Spends an afternoon splitting the root CLAUDE.md into topic files.
Developer's session still loads ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md as well.
New files still get the licence header.
Tidier project config; the real cause is untouched.

options.verdict: A worthwhile refactor that does not find the cause.
options.why: Modular rules help maintainability, but the problem is an unknown loaded file. Right pattern, wrong problem: diagnose with /memory before restructuring.

labs.takeaway: Behaviour differs between sessions or people → run /memory to see what is loaded before editing anything.

labs.title: Four API packages share one standard
labs.context: A monorepo has six packages, each with its own CLAUDE.md, and Claude Code reviews every PR in CI. The platform team maintains an error-response standard in docs/standards/errors.md that must apply to the four public-API packages only, both in CI reviews and in local sessions. The team wants one source of truth that it edits in one place.
labs.question: How should the standard be wired in?

options.text: Paste the current error-response standard into the CLAUDE.md of each of the four public-API packages and commit the copies.
options.code:
<!-- packages/orders-api/CLAUDE.md -->
## Error responses
- Return { code, message, traceId }.
- Use 422 for validation errors.
<!-- same text pasted into 3 more packages -->

trace.text: Platform team changes 422 to 400 in docs/standards/errors.md.
CI review of orders-api loads its pasted copy: still says 422.
Flags a correct 400 response as a violation.
Developers ignore the comment; copies keep drifting.

options.verdict: Four copies, and they go out of date the first time the standard changes.
options.why: Duplicated text drifts away from the source file. The constraint asks for one place to edit, which copies cannot give.

options.text: Put the standard in the CI runner's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so every automated review applies it to the API packages.
options.code:
# CI setup step
mkdir -p ~/.claude
cp docs/standards/errors.md ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
claude -p "Review this PR."

trace.text: CI reviews apply the standard to every package, including the 2 internal ones.
Flags internal CLI tools for missing traceId.
Developer runs Claude locally on orders-api: standard not loaded.
Local and CI results disagree.

options.verdict: Wrong packages in CI and nothing at all for local sessions.
options.why: User-level config belongs to one machine and is not scoped to packages. The standard must reach local sessions too and only four packages, so wrong scope.

options.text: Make the standard a project skill, /error-standard, and have the CI review prompt invoke it on every PR.
options.code:
# .github/workflows/review.yml (excerpt)
claude -p "Run /error-standard, then review
  this PR for problems." \
  --output-format json

trace.text: CI invokes /error-standard on every PR, including internal packages.
Applies API error rules to an internal batch tool.
Developer edits orders-api locally and never invokes the skill.
Local change returns a bare string error; nobody notices until CI.

options.verdict: CI gets it everywhere, local sessions only if someone remembers.
options.why: Skills load on demand, so a standard that must always apply in four packages is missed in normal work. Right pattern, wrong scope.

options.text: Keep docs/standards/errors.md as the one source and add an @import line for it to each public-API package's CLAUDE.md.
options.code:
<!-- packages/orders-api/CLAUDE.md -->
# Orders API
@../../docs/standards/errors.md

<!-- same import line in the other 3 API packages -->

trace.text: Platform team changes 422 to 400 in docs/standards/errors.md.
CI review of orders-api loads its CLAUDE.md plus the imported file.
Accepts the 400 response; flags one missing traceId.
Review of the internal batch tool: standard not loaded.
Local sessions in the API packages see the same text.

options.verdict: One source file feeds exactly the four packages, locally and in CI.
options.why: Importing a shared standards file into each package CLAUDE.md gives one source of truth scoped to the packages that need it. Project files are committed, so CI and local runs match.

labs.takeaway: One standard, several packages → @import a shared file into each package CLAUDE.md, never paste copies.

checks.q: A CI job ignores a coding standard that every developer sees locally. Where is the standard most likely stored?
checks.a: In each developer's user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. CI never receives that file, so the standard should move to project-level CLAUDE.md.

checks.q: Claude follows a rule in some sessions but not others. What is the first step?
checks.a: Run `/memory` to see which memory files are actually loaded, instead of rewording or repeating the rule.

checks.q: Five packages need the same API conventions. How do you avoid five copies?
checks.a: Keep one standards file and pull it into each package's CLAUDE.md with an `@` import.

currentNote: Current Claude Code also loads a managed-policy CLAUDE.md and a gitignored `CLAUDE.local.md`, and subdirectory files load on demand. All discovered files are concatenated rather than overriding each other, and the import syntax is a plain `@path/to/file` line.

spokes.note: Project level: whole team and CI

quiz.q: A developer's coding standard works in her sessions, but a teammate who joined this week never sees Claude follow it. What is the most likely cause?
options: The standard is in her user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, which is not shared
The teammate needs to restart Claude Code to refresh the project memory
The standard needs stronger wording such as IMPORTANT to be honoured
Directory-level files override the project file in the teammate's folder
quiz.why: User-level config is not version-controlled, so only its owner receives it. Moving the standard to project-level CLAUDE.md shares it with the team.

quiz.q: Claude applies the API naming rules in some sessions and ignores them in others. What should you do first?
options: Repeat the naming rules in every package CLAUDE.md
Rewrite the rules in capital letters at the top of the file
Run `/memory` to see which memory files are actually loaded
Move the naming rules into a skill so they can be invoked
quiz.why: Inconsistent behaviour is a loading question. `/memory` shows what is loaded instead of guessing with emphasis or duplication.

quiz.q: Six packages in a monorepo need the same security standards. What keeps them consistent?
options: Paste the standards text into each package CLAUDE.md file
Keep one standards file and `@`-import it in each package CLAUDE.md
Put the standards in each developer's user-level CLAUDE.md file
Turn the standards into a skill that each package can call
quiz.why: An import keeps one source of truth. Copies drift, user-level files are not shared, and a skill loads only on demand.

quiz.q: Your CLAUDE.md is long, so a colleague suggests moving the "never log personal data" rule into a skill. Why is this a poor idea?
options: Skills cannot contain rules about logging or personal data
Skills are user-level only, so the team would lose the rule
Skills always load, so the context would not shrink at all
Skills load only when invoked, so the rule would often be missing
quiz.why: A universal rule must be always loaded. Use `.claude/rules/` topic files or imports to split CLAUDE.md instead.

misconceptions.myth: A subfolder CLAUDE.md overrides the root CLAUDE.md.
misconceptions.fact: Files are concatenated, not overridden. If they contradict, Claude may follow either, so remove the contradiction.

misconceptions.myth: If Claude ignores a rule, write it louder.
misconceptions.fact: Emphasis cannot fix a file that is not loaded or not shared. Check the level, then run `/memory`.

misconceptions.myth: My user-level CLAUDE.md reaches CI because CI uses Claude Code too.
misconceptions.fact: CI only gets files in the repository. User-level files never leave your machine.

scenario.title: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
scenario.story:
Priya's team adds a Claude review step to their pipeline. Locally, Claude always checks that new endpoints have rate limiting. In CI it never does.

The first idea is to put **MUST CHECK RATE LIMITING** in bold in the prompt. Tom stops them and asks a simpler question: where does the rule live? Priya runs `/memory` on her laptop. The rule is in her `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, a file that has never been in git. Her teammates had copied parts of it by hand, which is why it seemed to work for most of them.

They move the rule to the root `CLAUDE.md` and commit it. The API package already had its own `CLAUDE.md` with an older copy of the endpoint rules, so they delete that copy and replace it with `@docs/standards/api.md`, a shared file the root also imports.

The next pipeline run flags a missing rate limit on the first PR. New starters get the rule on day one, and there is now one file to update when the policy changes.

plain: Slash commands and skills are saved, reusable workflows, such as "review this PR" or "write a changelog". Claude runs them only when they are needed, so they do not fill every session with instructions. A skill has a small settings block at the top (frontmatter) that controls how it runs.
analogy: A skill is like a recipe card in a drawer. You take it out only when you cook that dish, unlike the house rules pinned to the fridge (CLAUDE.md) that apply every day.

sections.body:
**A skill is a saved workflow that loads only when the task needs it.**

Think of jobs you repeat: "review this PR", "write release notes", "audit dependencies". Instead of typing the steps each time, you save them once.

- A **command** is a Markdown file in `.claude/commands/`, run by typing `/name`.
- A **skill** is a folder with a `SKILL.md` file in `.claude/skills/<name>/`. It has YAML frontmatter at the top that controls how it runs. Claude can also pick a skill on its own when the task matches its `description`.

In current Claude Code, commands have been merged into skills. Old command files still work, but new work should use skills.

CLAUDE.md is different: it is **always loaded**. Skills cost no context until they are used.

**Commit it if the team or CI needs it; keep it in your home folder if only you do.**

| Where | Who gets it |
|---|---|
| `.claude/skills/` or `.claude/commands/` | Everyone, through git |
| `~/.claude/skills/` or `~/.claude/commands/` | Only you |

Want a shorter version of the team's `review-pr` skill? Create `~/.claude/skills/my-quick-review/SKILL.md` with a **different name**. Editing the shared skill changes it for every teammate.

The reverse mistake is putting a team workflow in `~/.claude/commands/` and asking people to copy it. Copies drift, new starters miss it, and CI never sees it.

sections.h: Frontmatter options and the symptoms they fix
sections.body:
**Each frontmatter option answers one specific problem.**

```yaml
---
name: dependency-audit
description: Audit dependencies and write a report.
argument-hint: [package-dir]
context: fork
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob Write
---
```

- **Output floods the session** → `context: fork` runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent. Only the result comes back.
- **The skill must not use certain tools** → `allowed-tools`, a space-separated list. This is configuration, not a polite request in the text.
- **The skill needs input** → `argument-hint` shows what to pass, and `$ARGUMENTS` receives it.

Other fields include `model` and `disable-model-invocation`, which stops Claude starting the skill by itself.

**Needed in most sessions → CLAUDE.md. Needed for one job → skill.**

A quick test: would this instruction matter if someone opened Claude Code to fix a random bug?

- **Yes** → it is a universal standard. Put it in CLAUDE.md, which is always loaded.
- **No, only when doing that job** → put it in a skill, which loads on demand.

What goes wrong:

- An occasional release-notes workflow in CLAUDE.md wastes context in every session.
- A universal security rule in a skill is missing whenever nobody invokes the skill.
- "Please don't use Bash" written in the skill body is probabilistic. Claude may still use it. Use `allowed-tools` instead.
- A huge analysis skill without `context: fork` floods the main session.

example.title: Worked example: a team dependency-audit skill
example.code:
---
name: dependency-audit
description: Audit package dependencies for outdated or risky versions and write a report.
argument-hint: [package-dir]
context: fork
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob Write
---

# Dependency audit

1. Read the package.json in the directory given as $ARGUMENTS.
2. List each dependency with its pinned version.
3. Flag anything more than one major version behind.
4. Write the findings to reports/deps-audit.md.
5. Return a 5-line summary to the main session.
notes: The file sits at `.claude/skills/dependency-audit/SKILL.md`, so it is shared with the team through the repo.
`argument-hint` shows the user that a package directory is expected.
`context: fork` runs the long audit in an isolated sub-agent, so only the short summary returns.
`allowed-tools` is a space-separated list. It limits the skill to reading, searching and writing files, so it should not run shell commands.
`$ARGUMENTS` is replaced with whatever the user types after `/dependency-audit`; `$0`, `$1` pick out single arguments.

labs.title: Docs skill deletes files with a shell
labs.context: The team's update-docs project skill should only read source code and write Markdown files. Last week, during a run, it used the shell to delete docs/old/, including a hand-written guide. The team wants the skill to be limited to reading and writing files whenever it runs, without changing how other work in the session behaves.
labs.question: What change best meets this requirement?

options.text: Add a clear instruction to the skill body saying it must never use Bash and may only read code and write Markdown.
options.code:
---
name: update-docs
description: Refresh docs from source code.
---

IMPORTANT: Do not use Bash. Only read code
and write .md files.

trace.text: /update-docs
Reads src/api.ts and decides old docs should be cleared first.
Bash: rm -rf docs/old/   (nothing stops it)
docs/old/ deleted again, including the hand-written guide.

options.verdict: The instruction was ignored once, and nothing stopped it.
options.why: Instructions are probabilistic, so a skill told not to use a tool can still use it. Probabilistic fix where an enforced limit is needed.

options.text: Add allowed-tools to the skill's SKILL.md frontmatter, listing only the read, search and write tools the skill needs.
options.code:
---
name: update-docs
description: Refresh docs from source code.
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob Write
---

Read the source and update the matching
Markdown files under docs/.

trace.text: /update-docs
Reads src/api.ts with Read and Grep.
Bash is outside this skill's allowed-tools, so the skill does not use it.
Writes docs/api.md with Write.
Docs updated; no shell commands run.

options.verdict: The skill works within read and write tools only.
options.why: For the exam, allowed-tools restricts which tools a skill may use while it runs, so the limit no longer depends on Claude obeying a sentence. In current Claude Code it mainly pre-approves the listed tools, so add a permission deny rule if Bash must be blocked outright.

options.text: Move the docs workflow into the project CLAUDE.md with a "never use Bash for docs" rule so it is always in context.
options.code:
<!-- CLAUDE.md (always loaded) -->
## Updating docs
When asked to update docs, read the
source, never use Bash, and only write
.md files under docs/.

trace.text: Every session loads the docs workflow, even for unrelated bug fixes.
Update the docs for the API.
Follows the text, but nothing limits its tools.
Bash: mv docs/api.md docs/api.old.md

options.verdict: Wastes context in every session and still does not limit tools.
options.why: CLAUDE.md is always loaded, so an occasional workflow costs context everywhere. It is still only an instruction, so the tools are not limited.

options.text: Add context: fork to the skill's frontmatter so it runs in an isolated sub-agent that cannot touch the main session.
options.code:
---
name: update-docs
description: Refresh docs from source code.
context: fork
---

Read the source and update docs/.

trace.text: /update-docs
Skill runs in a forked sub-agent context.
Bash: rm -rf docs/old/   (the fork still has shell access)
Main session context stays clean; docs/old/ is gone anyway.

options.verdict: The context is isolated, but the files are still deleted.
options.why: context: fork isolates conversation context, not tools or the file system. Right pattern, wrong problem.

labs.takeaway: A skill must be limited to certain tools → allowed-tools in SKILL.md, not an instruction in its body.

labs.title: One developer wants a different scaffold
labs.context: The team shares a /scaffold-module project skill that generates boilerplate for new modules in a legacy monorepo. One developer wants a version that also writes a README stub and puts tests in a __tests__ folder, which suits only his workflow. Teammates and the CI job that uses the shared skill must see no change.
labs.question: Where should his version live?

options.text: Edit the shared .claude/skills/scaffold-module/SKILL.md to add the README stub and the __tests__ layout, then commit it.
options.code:
<!-- .claude/skills/scaffold-module/SKILL.md -->
...
- Also write README.md with a TODO stub.
- Put tests in __tests__/ next to the module.

trace.text: Change merged to main.
Teammate runs /scaffold-module: gets an unexpected __tests__ folder.
CI job scaffolds a module; test runner finds no tests in tests/.
Two teammates revert the change.

options.verdict: His preference changes behaviour for the whole team and CI.
options.why: The shared project skill is used by everyone through version control. Editing it for one person breaks the stated constraint.

options.text: Add his preferences to his ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, telling Claude to add a README stub and __tests__ whenever it scaffolds a module.
options.code:
<!-- ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md -->
## When scaffolding modules
- Also write README.md with a TODO stub.

scenario.title: Developer Productivity with Claude
scenario.story:
Marco built a `pr-summary` skill for his team. It reads the diff, the linked ticket and recent commits, then writes a summary. People liked it, but three problems appeared.

First, the skill dumped every file it read into the conversation, so developers lost track of their own work. Marco added `context: fork`, and now only the finished summary comes back.

Second, it once ran `git push` while "tidying up". The skill text already said "never push", so writing it again would not help. Marco added `allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob` to the frontmatter.

Third, people forgot to give a PR number. An `argument-hint: [pr-number]` line now shows them what to type.

Then Aisha wanted bullet points instead of prose. She almost edited the shared file, which would have changed it for everyone. Instead she created `~/.claude/skills/pr-summary-bullets/` with a new name. The team skill stayed the same, and both versions now do their job.

plain: A path-specific rule is a small instructions file that only switches on when Claude works on matching files, such as every `*.test.tsx` file. You write the file pattern (a "glob") at the top of the rule. The rest of the time it stays out of Claude's context and costs nothing.
analogy: It is like a safety notice that lights up only when you pick up a power tool. You never see it while making tea, but it is always there when it matters.

sections.body:
**A rule with `paths` globs loads only when Claude works on matching files.**

Rules are Markdown files in `.claude/rules/`, such as `.claude/rules/terraform.md`. At the top you can add YAML frontmatter with a `paths` list:

```yaml
---
paths:
  - "terraform/**/*"
  - "**/*.test.tsx"
---
```

A **glob** is a file pattern:

- `*` means any name, so `*.tf` matches every Terraform file in one folder.
- `**` means any number of folders, so `**/*.test.tsx` matches test files anywhere.
- Braces work too: `src/**/*.{ts,tsx}`.

A rules file **without** `paths` loads in every session, just like CLAUDE.md. Adding globs is how you scope it.

sections.h: How it works step by step
sections.body:
**Matching happens automatically; nobody has to call the rule.**

1. You save `.claude/rules/react-tests.md` with `paths: - "**/*.test.tsx"` and commit it.
2. A teammate starts Claude Code. The rule is **not** in context yet.
3. They ask Claude to fix the header colour in `src/Header.tsx`. No match, so no test guidance is loaded.
4. Next they ask for a new test. Claude opens `src/cart/Cart.test.tsx`, the path matches, and the rule loads.
5. Claude writes the test following the team's conventions.

Compare this with a skill: a skill only loads when it is invoked. A path rule loads whenever the file matches, which is why it suits conventions that must always apply to a file type.

sections.h: When to use it, and when not to
sections.body:
**Pick by how the files are spread: by pattern across folders, or all in one folder.**

Use a path rule when a convention follows a **file type or pattern**:

- Test files sitting next to the code in 40 folders.
- Terraform, SQL migrations or GraphQL schemas with their own style.

Use a **directory-level CLAUDE.md** when the convention is confined to **one folder**, such as `packages/billing/`.

Keep a rule **without** `paths` (or in CLAUDE.md) when it applies to almost every task, such as "never commit secrets".

The gain is twofold: Claude is not distracted by unrelated guidance, and you spend fewer tokens on every task that does not touch those files.

**Each wrong answer either loads the rule too often or not at all.**

- **Root CLAUDE.md with "only applies to Terraform files".** The text still loads for every task. It wastes context and relies on Claude honouring the qualifier.
- **A CLAUDE.md in every test folder.** Forty copies multiply and drift, and a new folder gets none.
- **Packaging the convention as a skill.** Skills load only when called, so the convention is missed whenever nobody calls it.
- **Moving the rule to user level to stop it loading.** That removes it for every teammate instead of scoping it.
- **Putting anything above the opening `---`.** Frontmatter must be the first thing in the file, or the `paths` list is ignored and the rule loads everywhere.

example.title: Worked example: a rule for React test files
example.code:
---
paths:
  - "**/*.test.tsx"
---

# React test conventions

- Use React Testing Library; do not use Enzyme.
- Query by role or label, not by CSS class.
- One `describe` block per component.
- Mock network calls with msw handlers from `test/handlers.ts`.
- Each test must assert on visible behaviour, not internal state.
notes: The file is saved as `.claude/rules/react-tests.md` and committed with the project.
The `paths` glob `**/*.test.tsx` matches test files in any folder, wherever they sit.
When Claude edits `src/cart/Cart.tsx` (not a test), this rule stays unloaded.
Removing the frontmatter would make the rule load in every session again.

scenario.title: Code Generation with Claude Code
scenario.story:
Leah's team has a monorepo with React apps, a Node API and a `terraform/` folder. Their root CLAUDE.md had grown to 600 lines, half of it about Terraform tagging and test conventions.

Front-end developers noticed Claude sometimes added `owner` tags to React props, mixing up the two sets of rules. Every task also carried all 600 lines.

Leah's first idea was a CLAUDE.md in each test folder. She counted 37 folders and dropped it. Her second idea was a `terraform-style` skill, but a colleague pointed out that nobody would remember to call it before editing a `.tf` file.

She created two files. `.claude/rules/terraform.md` starts with `paths:` and `- "terraform/**/*"`. `.claude/rules/react-tests.md` uses `- "**/*.test.tsx"`. She removed both sections from the root file and committed.

Now a header fix loads neither rule. Editing `terraform/storage/main.tf` loads the tagging rule automatically. The root CLAUDE.md is down to 120 lines, and the odd tag suggestions in React code have stopped.

plain: Plan mode means Claude first looks around and writes a plan, without changing any files, so you can agree the approach. Direct execution means Claude just makes the change. Big or uncertain jobs need a plan first; small, obvious fixes do not.
analogy: Rewiring a whole house starts with a drawing that everyone signs off. Changing a light bulb does not need a drawing; you just change it.

sections.body:
**Plan mode looks and proposes; direct execution changes files.**

- **Plan mode**: Claude reads code, searches and thinks, but does **not** edit files. It ends with a proposed approach for you to approve. Start it with `claude --permission-mode plan`, press Shift+Tab to cycle modes, or type `/plan`.
- **Direct execution**: Claude edits files as it goes. This is the normal way of working.

The recommended pattern for big jobs is **plan first, then execute**:

1. Plan mode: investigate and compare approaches.
2. You pick one.
3. Leave plan mode and let Claude implement the chosen approach.

Staying in plan mode for the whole task is a mistake, because nothing ever gets built.

**Many files or more than one sensible approach → plan mode.**

Plan first when any of these is true:

- **Large scale**: a library migration touching 45+ files.
- **Several valid approaches**: two integration options with different infrastructure needs.
- **Architecture**: splitting a monolith into microservices.
- **Multi-file changes** where the order and shape of edits matter.

"Git can roll it back" is not a reason to skip planning. Rollback undoes edits, but it does not tell you which approach was right. You would just repeat the same 45-file change a second time.

A plan gives you a cheap point to say "not that way" before any file is touched.

**One file and one obvious fix → just do it.**

Use direct execution for well-scoped changes:

- A single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace.
- Adding one validation check.
- Renaming a variable inside one function.

Planning these adds a round trip and extra tokens without lowering any risk. The plan would simply say "add the null check", which you already knew.

A quick test from the exam tip: **count the files and count the valid approaches**. One and one means execute.

If a "small" fix turns out to touch many files, stop and switch to plan mode at that point.

sections.h: The Explore subagent solves a different problem
sections.body:
**Too much discovery output → Explore subagent, not plan mode.**

Long investigations read dozens of files and logs. All that output fills the main context until Claude starts losing track of earlier details. This is **context exhaustion**.

Plan mode does not help here. It stops edits; it does not shrink output.

The **Explore subagent** runs the discovery in its own separate context and hands back a short **summary**. The main session keeps room for the real work.

- Competing approaches → plan mode.
- Flood of discovery output → Explore subagent.
- Both at once → plan mode, with Explore doing the heavy reading.

example.title: Worked example: plan, then execute a library migration
example.code:
# Step 1: start in plan mode (no edits allowed)
$ claude --permission-mode plan
> Migrate from moment.js to date-fns across the repo.

Claude (plan):
  - Found 47 files importing moment.
  - Option A: direct date-fns calls everywhere.
  - Option B: thin wrapper src/lib/dates.ts, then swap imports.
  - Recommend B: one place to fix time-zone handling.

> Go with option B.

# Step 2: switch to direct execution (Shift+Tab)
Claude: creating src/lib/dates.ts ...
Claude: updating 47 imports ...
Claude: running npm test ... 312 passed.
notes: `--permission-mode plan` starts the session in plan mode, so Claude only investigates and proposes.
The plan surfaces two valid approaches; that choice is exactly what plan mode is for.
After approval, switching out of plan mode lets Claude implement the agreed option directly.
If the discovery step had produced huge output, an Explore subagent could return a summary instead.

labs.title: One null check, clear stack trace
labs.context: Production logs show a TypeError, and the stack trace points at one undefined property access on line 42 of a single profile file. The cause is clear: the user object is missing when a session has expired, and the fix is a single null check. The team wants the fix shipped with as little overhead as possible.
labs.question: How should the developer run Claude Code for this fix?

options.text: Use direct execution: give Claude the file, the line and the stack trace, and let it make and test the change.
options.code:
$ claude
> Fix the TypeError at src/user/profile.ts:42.
> Stack trace: user is undefined when the
> session has expired.

trace.text: Reads src/user/profile.ts around line 42.
Adds a guard that redirects to login when user is missing.
npm test -- profile: 12 passed.
Fix done in about a minute.

options.verdict: Quick, correct fix with no wasted steps.
options.why: One file, one obvious approach and a clear stack trace make this a well-scoped change. Direct execution is right for that.

options.text: Start in plan mode so Claude investigates the session handling first, then approve the plan and switch to implementation.
options.code:
$ claude --permission-mode plan
> Fix the TypeError at src/user/profile.ts:42.
> Investigate session handling before
> proposing a change.

trace.text: Investigates profile.ts, session handling and auth middleware.
Plan: "Add a null check at line 42."
Approves the obvious plan.
Leaves plan mode and adds the same null check.
Same result, an extra round trip and extra tokens.

options.verdict: It works, but planning added cost without reducing any risk.
options.why: Plan mode is for many files or competing approaches, and here there is one clear fix. Over-engineered.

options.text: Use plan mode for the whole task, refining the plan until it is complete, so nothing changes before it is fully reviewed.
options.code:
$ claude --permission-mode plan
> Fix the TypeError at src/user/profile.ts:42.
> Keep refining the plan until it is perfect.
> Do not leave plan mode.

trace.text: Proposes a plan with a null check.
Asks for more detail.
Refines the plan; plan mode does not edit files.
After 15 minutes, the bug is still in production.

options.verdict: Nothing is ever implemented.
options.why: Once an approach is chosen, direct execution should carry it out. Staying in plan mode stalls the work.

options.text: Have the Explore subagent map the authentication and session modules first, then fix the line using its summary.
options.code:
$ claude
> Use the Explore subagent to map the auth
> and session modules, summarise how users
> are loaded, then fix profile.ts:42.

trace.text: Delegates exploration of 38 auth and session files.
Explore returns a two-page summary of the auth flow.
Adds the same null check at line 42.
Correct fix after several extra minutes of discovery.

options.verdict: Correct in the end, but the discovery phase was unnecessary.
options.why: The Explore subagent protects context during long, multi-phase discovery. A one-line fix with a clear stack trace needs no discovery phase, so this is over-engineered.

labs.takeaway: Single file, clear stack trace, one obvious fix → direct execution.

labs.title: Auth client survey loses earlier services
labs.context: A developer uses Claude Code in plan mode to find every place that 30 services call an internal auth client, before replacing it. By the 18th service the session has compacted its context, and the draft plan omits call sites in services Claude had already surveyed. The plan must list every call site before any edit is made.
labs.question: What change best lets the survey finish with a complete list?

options.text: Stay in plan mode for the remaining services, because plan mode does not edit files and so keeps the session context small.
options.code:
> Continue in plan mode.
> Survey services 19 to 30 for calls
> to AuthClient. Read every file that
> imports it.

trace.text: Reads 140 more files into the main session.
Context compacted again.
Draft plan lists 61 call sites; services 3 and 7 are missing.
The developer cannot trust the plan.

options.verdict: Plan mode prevents edits, not context growth.
options.why: Plan mode does not isolate verbose output, so everything read still lands in the main context. Right pattern, wrong problem.

options.text: Switch to direct execution and start replacing the client in the 17 services already surveyed, so less needs to be read.
options.code:
> Leave plan mode.
> Replace AuthClient in the services
> you have already surveyed, then
> continue with the rest.

trace.text: Edits services 1 to 17 from its compacted notes.
Tests: 9 failures in services 3 and 7, where call sites were missed.
Half-migrated codebase; the changes are reverted.

options.verdict: Edits start before the call-site list is complete.
options.why: The constraint says the plan must be complete before any edit. Direct execution sidesteps the context problem by skipping the investigation the task needs.

options.text: Run /clear after every five services and paste a hand-written list of the call sites found so far back into the session.
options.code:
> /clear
> Call sites so far (pasted):
> - billing: 4, orders: 6, ...
> Now survey services 6 to 10.

trace.text: Copies notes, runs /clear, pastes notes back.
Surveys five more services; context fills again.
Writes the next list by hand and drops two entries.
Plan is built on incomplete manual notes.

options.verdict: Each batch still floods the context, and the notes lose detail.
options.why: Manual resets treat the symptom and depend on a person summarising correctly. The verbose file reading itself needs to happen outside the main session.

options.text: Delegate each group of services to the Explore subagent, so its file reading stays isolated and only summaries return.
options.code:
> Use the Explore subagent to survey
> services 1 to 10 for AuthClient calls.
> Return a table: service, file, line,
> method used. Repeat for 11-20, 21-30.

trace.text: Delegates services 1 to 10 to the Explore subagent.
Explore reads 120 files in its own context.
Returns a 25-row table of call sites.
Repeats for 11-20 and 21-30; the main context holds only three tables.
Plan lists all 74 call sites before any edit.

options.verdict: The survey completes and nothing earlier is lost.
options.why: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery output and returns summaries, which prevents context exhaustion. Plan mode stays in use for the overall decision.

labs.takeaway: Verbose discovery is filling context → Explore subagent, not a mode switch.

labs.title: Every labelled issue waits for plan approval
labs.context: A CI workflow runs Claude Code on any issue labelled "claude-fix", always in plan mode, and waits for a human to approve the plan before implementing. One-line fixes with a clear cause, such as a wrong error message, now wait two to three days for approval. Larger issues that touch many files or have several valid approaches must still be planned and approved first.
labs.question: How should the workflow be changed?

options.text: Keep plan mode for every issue but approve plans automatically, so small fixes no longer wait for a human.
options.code:
# .github/workflows/claude-fix.yml (excerpt)
- run: claude -p "Plan issue $N" --permission-mode plan
- run: echo "auto-approved"
- run: claude -p "Implement the plan for issue $N"

trace.text: Typo fix ships in 10 minutes.
Large issue: plans a new caching layer touching 26 files.
Plan auto-approved; 26 files changed.
Architecture lead rejects the approach after merge.

options.verdict: Small fixes are faster, but large changes lose their approval gate.
options.why: The constraint says larger issues must still be approved before implementation. Automatic approval keeps the planning cost but removes the review it exists for.

options.text: Use direct execution for every issue and rely on normal PR review to catch any change that took the wrong approach.
options.code:
# .github/workflows/claude-fix.yml (excerpt)
- run: |
    claude -p "Fix issue $N and open a PR." \
      --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash"

trace.text: Typo fix ships in 10 minutes.
Large issue: picks one of two valid approaches and edits 31 files.
Reviewer prefers the other approach.
PR closed; the 31-file change is redone.

options.verdict: Small fixes are fast, but large ones are built before the approach is agreed.
options.why: Review after the fact does not choose between valid approaches before the work. Multi-file changes with competing approaches need plan mode first.

options.text: Route by scope: clear single-file fixes use direct execution; multi-file or multi-approach issues get plan mode, approval, then direct execution.
options.code:
# .github/workflows/claude-fix.yml (excerpt)
- if: contains(labels, 'scope:small')
  run: claude -p "Fix issue $N and open a PR."
- if: "!contains(labels, 'scope:small')"
  run: claude -p "Plan issue $N" --permission-mode plan
# after plan-approved label: implement directly

trace.text: Wrong-error-message issue is triaged scope:small.
Direct execution: fixes one string, tests pass, PR in 10 minutes.
Caching issue: plan mode compares two approaches across 26 files.
Architecture lead approves one approach.
Second run implements the approved plan directly.

options.verdict: Small fixes ship fast; large changes are still agreed first.
options.why: Direct execution suits well-scoped changes, while multi-file or multi-approach work needs plan mode first. Combining the two keeps both speed and the approval gate.

options.text: Keep plan mode for every issue, but have the same plan-mode run carry out the change once its plan is written.
options.code:
# .github/workflows/claude-fix.yml (excerpt)
- run: |
    claude -p "Plan issue $N, then implement it." \
      --permission-mode plan

trace.text: Writes a plan for the typo fix.
Plan mode does not edit files; the run ends with a plan only.
No PR is opened for any issue.
Small fixes now wait forever instead of for days.

options.verdict: Nothing is implemented, small or large.
options.why: Plan mode is for settling the approach, not for carrying it out. Implementation needs direct execution once the plan is agreed.

labs.takeaway: Match the mode to the task: clear single-file fix → direct; multi-file or competing approaches → plan, then direct.

checks.a: Plan mode, to investigate and choose the approach, then direct execution to implement it.

checks.a: No. Plan mode does not isolate output. Use the Explore subagent, which works in its own context and returns a summary.

checks.q: Why is "git can roll it back" not a reason to skip planning on a large change?

scenario.title: Code Generation with Claude Code
scenario.story:
Sam's team needs to move from a home-grown HTTP client to `axios`. A quick search shows 48 files using the old client, and there are two ways to do it: swap every call directly, or add a small wrapper first.

Sam's first instinct is to tell Claude "replace it everywhere" and rely on git if it goes wrong. A senior colleague points out that git would only let them undo the change, not tell them which approach was better.

Sam starts `claude --permission-mode plan`. The investigation is large, so Claude hands the reading to an Explore subagent, which returns a one-page summary: 48 files, three special cases with custom retry logic. Claude proposes the wrapper approach so retry handling lives in one place.

The team agrees. Sam presses Shift+Tab to leave plan mode, and Claude builds `src/lib/http.ts`, updates the imports and runs the tests.

The next day a one-line timeout bug appears in the wrapper. Sam fixes it with direct execution in two minutes. No plan needed.

plain: Iterative refinement is how you steer Claude when its first attempt is not quite right. The trick is to pick the technique that matches the kind of miss: show examples, write a test, let Claude interview you, or group related problems into one message.
analogy: It is like giving directions to a taxi driver. If they keep misreading your description, show the address on a map (examples). If you are not sure where you are going, let them ask you questions (interview).

sections.body:
**Diagnose the kind of miss first, then pick the matching technique.**

Claude's first attempt is often close but not right. Iterative refinement is how you steer it the rest of the way. The mistake is to always do the same thing, usually writing a longer, louder description.

There are four common kinds of miss:

1. Claude reads your description a different way each time.
2. A **known** edge case fails, such as nulls in old rows.
3. You are in an unfamiliar area and do not yet **know** all the requirements.
4. There are several problems at once.

Each has its own fix, covered below. Two questions pick it: **is the requirement already known?** and **do the issues interact?**

sections.h: Examples and test cases for known requirements
sections.body:
**Show, do not describe: 2–3 input/output examples beat another paragraph.**

If Claude keeps misreading "format phone numbers internationally", more prose keeps the ambiguity. Give concrete pairs instead:

- `'07700 900123'` → `'+447700900123'`
- `'(07700) 900 123'` → `'+447700900123'`

For a **known edge case**, write a specific test with the exact input and expected output, for example `normalise_phone(None)` returns `None`.

**Test-driven iteration** takes this further:

1. Write tests for normal behaviour, edge cases and performance ("10,000 rows in under 2 seconds").
2. Ask Claude to implement.
3. Run the tests and iterate on the failures.

"Make it fast" in a prompt is not checkable. A performance test is.

sections.h: The interview pattern for unknown requirements
sections.body:
**When you do not know what to ask for, let Claude ask you.**

Suppose you are adding a cache to a service and have never built one. You might not think about cache invalidation, stale reads or what happens when the cache server is down.

The interview pattern means you say: "Before writing any code, ask me questions about anything you need to know." Claude then asks things like:

- When should a cached entry be thrown away?
- What should happen if the cache is unreachable?

Your answers become the requirements, and you can turn them into tests.

Do **not** use it for something you already know precisely. Interviewing about a null edge case you could write as a test just adds a slow round trip.

sections.h: Several issues: together or one at a time
sections.body:
**Interacting issues go in one detailed message; independent ones go one at a time.**

Issues **interact** when fixing one changes another. For example, a CSV importer parses dates as US format, uses the date as part of the de-duplication key, and drops duplicates before validating. Fix the date parsing alone and the de-dup key changes; fix the order alone and the parsing runs twice.

Send these together, explaining how they connect, so Claude designs one consistent change.

Issues are **independent** when they live in unrelated code, such as a typo in the footer and a slow report query. Fix them one by one, checking each.

What goes wrong: sending interacting fixes one per message. Each new fix quietly undoes the last, and you go round in circles.

example.title: Worked example: examples plus a specific edge-case test
example.code:
# Prompt to Claude (shown as a comment):
# "Write normalise_phone(). Examples:
#   '07700 900123'   -> '+447700900123'
#   '+44 7700-900123' -> '+447700900123'
#   '(07700) 900 123' -> '+447700900123'
#  Make these tests pass."

import pytest
from phones import normalise_phone

@pytest.mark.parametrize("raw, expected", [
    ("07700 900123", "+447700900123"),
    ("+44 7700-900123", "+447700900123"),
    ("(07700) 900 123", "+447700900123"),
])
def test_formats(raw, expected):
    assert normalise_phone(raw) == expected

def test_none_returns_none():
    # known edge case: null input from legacy rows
    assert normalise_phone(None) is None
notes: Three concrete input/output pairs replace a vague description such as "convert to international format".
The parametrised test turns those examples into a checkable target.
`test_none_returns_none` pins down a known edge case with its exact expected output.
Claude iterates by running `pytest` and fixing failures, not by guessing what you meant.

labs.title: Three importer bugs that affect each other
labs.context: A CSV importer has three bugs: dates are parsed in US format, the raw date column is used as the de-duplication key, and duplicates are dropped before validation. Each fix changes the input to the next step, so fixing one alters the others. The developer already knows the correct behaviour for all three.
labs.question: How should the developer give these issues to Claude?

options.text: Send one bug per message and wait for tests to pass before sending the next, so each change is small and reviewable.
options.code:
Message 1: Fix date parsing to UK format.
(later) Message 2: De-dup on customer_id + date.
(later) Message 3: Validate before de-dup.
(each sent after the previous tests pass)

trace.text: Fix 1: switches to UK date parsing. Tests pass.
Fix 2: builds the de-dup key from the raw date string.
pytest: same-day rows in different formats not merged.
Fix 3: moves validation, which re-parses dates the old way.
pytest: date parsing test fails again.

options.verdict: Each fix breaks another; the loop goes round in circles.
options.why: Sequential iteration suits independent issues only. Interacting defects fixed one at a time undo each other.

options.text: Describe all three bugs in one detailed message that explains how they depend on each other and includes a shared test.
options.code:
Three linked issues in importer.py; fix together:
1. Parse dates as DD/MM/YYYY (UK), not MM/DD.
2. De-duplicate on (customer_id, parsed_date),
   so it depends on fix 1.
3. Validate rows BEFORE de-duplication.
Test: 03/04/2025 and 2025-04-03 for the same
customer must count as one row.

trace.text: Reads importer.py and sees how parsing, de-dup and validation connect.
Changes parse order, key and validation in one consistent edit.
pytest: 18 passed, including the duplicate-date test.
All three issues fixed in one round.

options.verdict: One coherent fix that holds together.
options.why: Interacting issues belong in one detailed message, so Claude can design one change that satisfies all three. Sending them separately lets each fix undo the last.

options.text: Ask Claude to interview the developer about date handling, duplicates and validation before it changes any code.
options.code:
Before changing importer.py, interview me
about anything you need to know about
date handling, duplicates and validation.
Ask one question at a time.

trace.text: Asks: which date format? What is a duplicate? Validate when?
Answers with what he already knew: UK, customer plus date, validate first.
Then implements the combined fix.
Works, but took an extra round for known facts.

options.verdict: It gets there, but the interview added nothing new.
options.why: The interview pattern surfaces unknown considerations, and here the requirements were already known. Right pattern, wrong problem.

options.text: Give Claude three input/output examples of correctly parsed dates and let it work out the de-duplication and validation fixes.

trace.text: Fixes date parsing to match the examples.
Leaves the de-dup key on the raw date string.
pytest: duplicates in mixed date formats still imported twice.
Validation still runs after de-duplication.

options.verdict: One bug fixed; the two that depend on it are untouched.
options.why: Examples fix inconsistent interpretation of one rule, but the problem here is three interacting defects. Right pattern, wrong problem.

labs.takeaway: Interacting issues → one detailed message; independent issues → one at a time.

labs.title: Data-retention job in an unfamiliar domain
labs.context: A developer must have Claude Code build a nightly job that purges old customer records from a legacy database. The ticket says only "delete records older than seven years", nobody on the team has built a retention job before, and nobody has asked legal about exceptions. The job must be right before it touches production data.
labs.question: What should the developer do before Claude implements the job?

options.text: Write a detailed prose specification of the purge rules the team knows, with emphasis on safety, and ask Claude to implement it.
options.code:
Build purge_expired.py. Delete customer
records older than 7 years. BE VERY CAREFUL.
Never delete anything important.
Log every deletion.

trace.text: Implements a purge on created_at older than 7 years.
Staging run deletes 1,240 records.
37 of them were under a legal hold.
Audit finding; job disabled.

options.verdict: The spec only contains what the team already knew.
options.why: More detailed prose cannot include considerations nobody has thought of. "Be careful" does not surface legal holds.

options.text: Give Claude three input/output examples of records that should and should not be purged, then let it implement the job.
options.code:
Examples:
2016 record, inactive  -> purge
2023 record, active    -> keep
2017 record, active    -> keep
Implement purge_expired.py to match.

trace.text: Implements rules that fit all three examples.
Staging run passes the three examples.
Shared household records are deleted for both customers.

options.verdict: The examples cover only cases the team already understood.
options.why: Examples remove ambiguity in a known rule. They cannot reveal unknown requirements such as shared records (right pattern, wrong problem).

options.text: Ask Claude to interview the team about the domain first, surfacing exceptions and failure modes before implementing.
options.code:
Before writing any code, interview me about
data retention for this system. Ask about
failure modes, exceptions and anything we
may not have considered. Then propose a design.

trace.text: Asks: are any records under legal hold? Can records be shared between customers?
Checks with legal: yes, holds exist in a separate table.
Asks: should deletions be reversible for 30 days? Audit trail?
Implements a purge that skips held and shared records, with soft delete.
Staging run: 1,203 purged, 37 held, 0 wrongly deleted.

options.verdict: Unknown requirements are found before any code is written.
options.why: In an unfamiliar domain, the interview pattern has Claude ask questions that surface considerations the team has not thought of. That is exactly the gap here.

options.text: Let Claude implement the job straight away, run it against a staging copy, and fix the problems that show up there.
options.code:
> Build purge_expired.py for records
> past retention.
$ python purge_expired.py --db staging
> Fix whatever looks wrong.

trace.text: Implements a simple age-based purge.
Staging run completes with no errors.
Nobody knows legal holds exist, so nobody checks for them.
Job is promoted to production.

options.verdict: Problems nobody knows to look for are not found in staging.
options.why: Iterating on failures only works when someone can recognise a failure. Unknown requirements need to be surfaced before implementation.

labs.takeaway: Unfamiliar domain, unknown risks → interview pattern before implementing.

labs.title: PR summaries interpreted three different ways
labs.context: A CI job runs Claude Code to write a user-facing summary for each merged PR, which is published in the product changelog. The prompt asks for "a concise, user-facing summary", and after two rewrites of that wording the summaries still vary between one-word labels, technical paragraphs and marketing copy. The team knows exactly what a good summary looks like.
labs.question: What change most reliably makes the summaries consistent?

options.text: Add --output-format json with a --json-schema that defines a summary string field, so every run returns the same structure.
options.code:
claude -p "Write a concise, user-facing
  summary of this PR." \
  --output-format json \
  --json-schema '{"type":"object","properties":{"summary":{"type":"string"}}}'
