scenario.title: Developer Productivity with Claude
scenario.story:
Hana asks Claude to write a function that turns free-text delivery notes into a short label for drivers. Her description says "short, clear, no personal details". Every run gives a different style: sometimes a sentence, sometimes bullets, once with a phone number left in.

She rewrites the description twice, louder each time. Nothing changes.

A colleague suggests three examples instead. Hana pastes three real notes with the exact labels she wants, such as `"Leave with neighbour at no. 12, call 07700..."` → `"Neighbour no. 12"`. The style settles straight away.

She already knows one edge case: empty notes must produce `"No instructions"`. Rather than explaining it, she adds a test with that input and output.

Then she notices two linked problems. Labels are cut at 20 characters before personal details are removed, so half a phone number can survive. She sends both issues in one message, explaining that removal must happen before cutting. Claude changes the order in one edit and all tests pass.

plain: In CI/CD (the automated pipeline that tests and checks code), nobody is sitting at the keyboard to answer Claude. So Claude Code must run non-interactively, and its output must be in a format other tools can read. The right context and an independent reviewer keep the results useful and low-noise.
analogy: It is like leaving instructions for a night-shift worker. They cannot phone you with questions, so the job sheet must be complete, and their report must use the form the morning team can file.

sections.h: What changes when Claude runs in CI
sections.body:
**In a pipeline nobody can answer questions, and a program, not a person, reads the output.**

CI/CD is the automated system that builds, tests and checks code on every push or pull request. When Claude Code runs there, two things are different from your terminal:

- **No human is present.** If Claude waits for input, the job just sits there.
- **Output is consumed by tools.** A script may turn findings into inline PR comments, so the format must be exact every time.

Everything the run needs must also come from the repository: the prompt, the code, and project-level CLAUDE.md. Files on one developer's laptop are not there.

The rest of this lesson maps each pipeline symptom to one specific fix.

**Use `-p` (`--print`) so Claude runs the prompt, prints the result and exits.**

Step by step:

1. The pipeline runs `claude -p "Review pr.diff against CLAUDE.md"`.
2. Claude reads the files it needs and does the work.
3. It prints the answer to standard output.
4. The process exits with a status code the pipeline can check.

Without `-p`, Claude Code opens an interactive session and waits for input that never comes. The job **hangs** until it times out.

Adding a timeout or piping in fake input only hides the symptom. `-p` removes the cause.

You can also limit tools for the run, for example `--allowedTools "Read,Grep"` for a read-only review.

**Flags make the format deterministic; asking nicely in the prompt does not.**

```bash
claude -p "Review the diff" \
  --output-format json \
  --json-schema "$(cat review-schema.json)" \
  | jq '.structured_output' > findings.json
```

- `--output-format json` wraps the run in a JSON object. The plain text answer is in `result`.
- `--json-schema` makes Claude return an object that matches your schema. It arrives in the `structured_output` field.
- Your script reads `structured_output` and posts each finding at the right `file` and `line`.

The wrong approach is "Reply ONLY in JSON" in the prompt, then a regex to dig it out. One stray sentence such as "Here are the findings:" and the parser breaks.

sections.h: Right context and an independent reviewer
sections.body:
**Give the run what it needs to avoid repeats, and never let code review itself.**

- **Duplicate comments on every push**: pass the prior findings and ask only for new or still-unaddressed issues.
- **Duplicate tests**: include the existing test files so Claude does not cover the same scenarios again.
- **Standards**: keep testing rules, what makes a valuable test and available fixtures in **project** CLAUDE.md. Local and CI runs then share one source. The CI user's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` is not in version control.
- **Weak review**: the session that wrote the code still holds its own reasoning and tends to agree with itself. Use a **fresh, independent** `claude -p` run with only the diff and the standards.

For GitHub, `anthropics/claude-code-action@v1` packages this setup.

**Read the symptom in the question; each one maps to one fix.**

| Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|
| Job hangs until timeout | `-p` / `--print` |
| Output will not parse | `--output-format json` + `--json-schema` |
| Same comments every push | Include prior findings |
| Tests repeat existing ones | Include existing test files |
| Standards missing in CI | Move them to project CLAUDE.md |
| Review misses obvious bugs | Independent instance, not the author session |

Watch for answers that treat a symptom instead: longer timeouts, stricter prompt wording, regex clean-up, or asking the same session to "double-check" its work. They may help once, but they fail again on the next run.

example.title: Worked example: a PR review job
example.code:
# .github/workflows/claude-review.yml (illustrative)
name: claude-review
on: pull_request
jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
      - name: Review diff
        env:
          ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
        run: |
          git diff origin/main...HEAD > pr.diff
          claude -p "Review pr.diff against CLAUDE.md. Prior findings are in prior.json; report only new or still-unaddressed issues." \
            --output-format json \
            --json-schema "$(cat .github/review-schema.json)" \
            | jq '.structured_output' > findings.json
      - run: node scripts/post-inline-comments.js findings.json
notes: `-p` makes the run non-interactive, so the job cannot hang waiting for input.
`--output-format json` with `--json-schema` returns a JSON envelope whose `structured_output` field holds the schema-validated findings; `jq` extracts it for the posting script.
The prompt points at prior findings and asks only for new or unaddressed issues, avoiding duplicate comments.
Standards come from the committed project CLAUDE.md, the same file developers use locally.
This is a fresh run that did not write the code, so it acts as an independent reviewer.
For a ready-made setup, the official `anthropics/claude-code-action@v1` GitHub Action (installed with `/install-github-app`) wraps the same CLI.

labs.title: Review findings the CI bot can post
labs.context: A pipeline runs Claude Code on every PR, and a script turns each finding into an inline comment using its file, line and message. The job must run unattended, and the script must be able to parse the output on every run without guessing. Findings will later feed a dashboard as well.
labs.question: How should the pipeline invoke Claude Code?

options.text: Run claude with the review prompt and ask in the prompt for a JSON array, then extract the array with a regex.
options.code:
claude "Review the diff. Reply ONLY in JSON:
  [{file, line, issue}]" > out.txt
# regex-extract the JSON array
node post.js out.txt

trace.text: CI starts claude without -p.
An interactive session opens and waits for input.
No input arrives; the job idles.
Job cancelled after the 60-minute timeout.

options.verdict: The job hangs, and the parsing would be fragile anyway.
options.why: Without -p, an unattended pipeline waits for input that never comes. JSON requested in the prompt is probabilistic, so regex parsing breaks eventually.

options.text: Run claude -p and ask in the prompt for a JSON array of findings, then parse the printed text with JSON.parse.
options.code:
claude -p "Review the diff. Reply ONLY in JSON:
  [{file, line, issue}]" > out.txt
# parse the printed text
node post.js out.txt

trace.text: CI runs claude -p; it completes and exits.
Returns "Here are the findings:" followed by a JSON block.
JSON.parse throws on the leading sentence.
No comments posted for this PR.

options.verdict: No more hang, but parsing fails on some runs.
options.why: -p fixes the hang, but formatting requested in the prompt is still probabilistic. Probabilistic where deterministic is needed.

options.text: Run claude -p with --output-format json and parse the result field, which holds Claude's reply text for each run.
options.code:
claude -p "Review the diff. List findings
  with file, line and issue." \
  --output-format json \
  | jq -r '.result' > findings.txt
node post.js findings.txt

trace.text: CI runs claude -p; the JSON envelope parses.
result field: a Markdown bullet list of findings.
post.js has to regex the bullets for file and line.
Line numbers written as "L42" on one run are dropped.

options.verdict: The wrapper is JSON, but the findings inside are still free text.
options.why: --output-format json alone wraps the reply in metadata; it does not shape the findings. Without a schema the script still parses prose.

options.text: Run claude -p with --output-format json and a --json-schema for each finding, then read the validated findings.
options.code:
claude -p "Review the diff against CLAUDE.md." \
  --output-format json \
  --json-schema "$(cat review-schema.json)" \
  | jq '.structured_output' > findings.json
node post.js findings.json

trace.text: CI runs claude -p; no prompt for input.
Reviews the diff against the project CLAUDE.md standards.
structured_output matches review-schema.json.
post.js posts 3 inline comments; the dashboard reads the same file.

options.verdict: Runs unattended, and the output parses every time.
options.why: A CI run needs -p, and output that feeds tools needs --output-format json with --json-schema. Both concerns are handled by flags, not by hoping the prompt is obeyed.

labs.takeaway: CI → -p; output feeds a tool → --output-format json with --json-schema.

labs.title: Ticket-driven tests repeat covered cases
labs.context: When a ticket moves to "Ready for test", a pipeline step runs Claude Code with -p to generate tests from the ticket text. For a refund-rounding ticket, most generated tests re-cover the full-refund path that the existing refunds test file already tests, while the ticket's three edge cases get none. The team wants generated tests to add coverage, not repeat it.
labs.question: What change most directly fixes this?

options.text: Add criteria for valuable tests and the list of payment fixtures to the project CLAUDE.md that the pipeline loads.
options.code:
<!-- CLAUDE.md -->
## Valuable tests
- Prefer edge cases over happy paths.
- Use fixtures from tests/fixtures/payments.
- Avoid trivial getter tests.

trace.text: Updated CLAUDE.md loaded by the pipeline run.
Writes tests for edge cases it guesses: zero amount, negative amount.
4 of 6 new tests duplicate cases in refunds.test.ts.
The ticket's three rounding cases still have no tests.

options.verdict: Better general guidance, but Claude still cannot see what exists.
options.why: Standards say what a good test is, but they cannot tell Claude which cases the existing file already covers. Right pattern, wrong problem.

options.text: Pass the existing refunds test file into the run alongside the ticket, and ask only for tests covering cases it lacks.
options.code:
cat tests/refunds.test.ts tickets/PAY-412.md | \
  claude -p "Above: the existing tests and the
  ticket. Write tests only for ticket cases the
  existing file does not cover. Reuse its fixtures."

trace.text: Reads refunds.test.ts: 14 existing cases, full refund covered.
Reads PAY-412: half-penny rounding, multi-currency, partial after discount.
Adds 3 tests, one per edge case, using existing fixtures.
npm test: 2 new tests fail and expose the rounding bug.

options.verdict: No duplicates, and the ticket's edge cases are covered.
options.why: Providing existing test files in context stops test generation from duplicating covered scenarios. With the ticket alongside, the new tests target the cases that matter.

options.text: Add a firm instruction to the pipeline prompt not to write duplicate tests and to concentrate on edge cases instead.
options.code:
claude -p "Write tests for ticket PAY-412.
  Do NOT duplicate existing tests.
  Focus on edge cases, not the happy path.
  Be thorough."

trace.text: Has not seen refunds.test.ts; guesses what exists.
Writes 8 tests; 5 overlap existing cases.
Only one of the ticket's edge cases is tested.

options.verdict: Claude cannot avoid duplicating tests it has never seen.
options.why: An instruction cannot replace missing context. Without the existing file, "do not duplicate" is only a guess.

options.text: Keep generating as now, then add a pipeline step that deletes new tests whose names match existing ones.
options.code:
# after generation
node scripts/dedupe-tests.js \
  --existing tests/refunds.test.ts \
  --new tests/refunds.generated.test.ts

trace.text: dedupe-tests removes 2 tests with matching names.
4 duplicates with different names remain.
The ticket's three edge cases are still untested.

options.verdict: Treats the symptom and still misses the real cases.
options.why: Post-processing cannot add tests that were never written, so the extra step is over-engineered. The fix is giving Claude the existing tests up front.

labs.takeaway: Generated tests duplicate existing ones → put the existing test files in context.

labs.title: Self-review keeps approving its own bugs
labs.context: A developer uses one Claude Code session to implement a new discount engine across eight files, then asks the same session to review the changes before opening a PR. The review has approved every change this month, yet QA has found four logic bugs that a reviewer should have caught. The team wants a more effective review without adding more human review time.
labs.question: What change most improves the review?

options.text: Keep the same session but tell it to review as a harsh senior engineer who assumes the code contains bugs.
options.code:
> Now review your changes as a harsh senior
> engineer. Assume there are bugs.
> Be critical. List every problem.
> Do not approve unless certain.

trace.text: Re-reads its own diff with its original reasoning in context.
Lists 6 style nits; "logic is correct as designed".
Stacked-discount bug ships to QA.

options.verdict: A sterner tone, the same blind spots.
options.why: The generating session retains its own reasoning and under-questions it, whatever the persona. Probabilistic fix for a structural problem.

options.text: Keep the same session but have it check each change against a detailed review checklist added to the project CLAUDE.md.
options.code:
<!-- CLAUDE.md -->
## Review checklist
- Check every branch for off-by-one errors.
- Check discount stacking and rounding.
- Check null inputs.

trace.text: Ticks each checklist item for its own code.
"Discount stacking: handled in applyDiscounts()."
QA: two percentage discounts compound instead of adding.
Bug ships despite a ticked checklist.

options.verdict: The checklist is applied by the same reasoning that wrote the bug.
options.why: A checklist helps an independent reviewer, but the author session still confirms its own assumptions. Right pattern, wrong problem.

options.text: Start a fresh Claude Code instance with no generation history to review the diff against the project standards.
options.code:
# new session, no generation history
git diff main...feature/discounts > diff.txt
claude -p "Review this diff against CLAUDE.md.
  Focus on logic errors." < diff.txt

trace.text: Independent reviewer reads only the diff and CLAUDE.md.
Flags: two percentage discounts compound instead of adding.
Flags: rounding happens before the cap is applied.
Developer fixes both before opening the PR.

options.verdict: The reviewer catches logic bugs the author missed.
options.why: The session that generated code reviews it less effectively than an independent instance. A fresh instance has no stake in the original reasoning.

options.text: Keep the same session but have it re-read every changed file in full before writing its review, instead of only the diff.
options.code:
> Before reviewing, re-read each of the
> 8 changed files in full, top to bottom.
> Then review the changes for logic errors.
> Cite line numbers.

trace.text: Reads all 8 files again.
Confirms the code matches its own plan.
Review approves; QA finds the rounding bug.

options.verdict: More reading, same author bias.
options.why: More context does not remove the author's bias, because the session still checks the code against its own intent. Right pattern, wrong problem.

labs.takeaway: Review quality matters → use an independent instance, not the session that wrote the code.

scenario.title: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
scenario.story:
Ollie's team adds an AI review step to their GitLab pipeline. In the first week three things go wrong.

Some jobs hang for an hour. The script called `claude "Review the diff"` without `-p`, so Claude opened an interactive session and waited. Adding `-p` fixed it.

Next, their comment poster crashed about one run in ten. They had asked for "JSON only" in the prompt and used a regex. They switched to `--output-format json` with `--json-schema "$(cat review-schema.json)"`, and the poster now reads the `structured_output` field. It has not crashed since.

Then developers complained that every push re-posted the same comments. The job now saves findings as an artifact, passes them into the next run, and asks only for new or still-open issues.

Finally, Ollie noticed the generation job and the review job shared one session. He split them, so the reviewer is a fresh `claude -p` run that sees only the diff and the project CLAUDE.md. In the first week it caught two bugs the old setup had approved.
